column6: Psalm 147 says that God takes no pleasure in a horse's strength or in human legs; it gives the commentary's running-horse figure a theological counterweight by refusing to make speed or power the ground of success.

column5: God delights in fear and hope
column6: The verse supplies the positive counterpart to the preceding horse image: YHWH delights in those who fear him and hope for his steadfast love, redirecting the running sequence toward trust rather than athletic advantage.
The psalmist says he will run in the way of God's commandments because God enlarges his heart; it makes the commentary's running movement an obedient, enabled course.
Proverbs promises that acknowledging God brings straight paths; its straightened route supplies a concise biblical analogue to S87:3's guidance and the commentary's smooth gait.

column5: led in right paths for the Name
column6: The shepherd restores and leads in paths of righteousness for the sake of his Name, combining the commentary's leader/follower motion with the Name named in S87:15.
YHWH identifies himself as the one who teaches what benefits and leads Israel in the way it should go; it is a particularly close covenantal formulation of “measured, then guided.”
The preparation of YHWH's way levels uneven ground and makes rough places a plain, giving the commentary's easy, well-placed footfall a concrete highway image.
In Isaiah's call to justice, the people's righteousness goes before them and YHWH's glory guards from behind; this ethical procession develops both ends of the commentary's moving line.

column5: stars brought out by number and called by name
column6: Isaiah asks who brings out the heavenly host by number and calls every star by name; it joins the commentary's stars in their courses to divine measuring, ordering, and command.

column5: Mazzaroth in season and Ayish guided
column6: God asks whether a human can bring Mazzaroth out in its season or guide Ayish with its children; this supplies a precise scriptural image of divine guidance of celestial bodies.

column5: statutes of moon and stars, stirred sea
column6: Jeremiah calls the regularity of moon and stars their fixed statutes while also naming the God who stirs the sea; its juxtaposition is a close biblical frame for the commentary's ordered stars and swimming-water imagery.

column5: Most High, Aramaic praise, lives forever
column6: In WLC's Aramaic numbering (often English Dan.4.34), the humbled king blesses the Most High, uses שַׁבְּחֵת for praise, and confesses the one who lives forever; it gathers the commentary's س ب ح, “Most High,” and enduring themes in a reversal of false sovereignty.

The commentary warns that preferring “the life of this world” misorders desire, whereas Deuteronomy commands Israel to choose life as covenant blessing; the contrast matters because the two texts give “life” different ethical functions.

column5: righteous live forever and have reward
column6: Wisdom's final vindication says that the righteous live forever and their reward is with the Lord, a Second Temple Jewish expression of the more abiding latter good.

The martyred brother expects the King of the universe to raise those dying for the law to an eternal renewal of life; its costly present action and enduring future outcome sharpen S87:16-17's comparison.

column5: World to Come without bodily consumption
column6: The rabbinic description of the World to Come removes eating, drinking, and ordinary worldly competition and has the righteous delight in divine radiance; it gives a concrete Jewish interpretation of a superior, lasting future state.

column5: guide our feet into the way of peace
column6: The Benedictus says that the dawn from on high will guide human feet into the way of peace, directly meeting S87:3's guidance and the commentary's attention to ordered footfall.

column5: run with endurance the race set before
column6: Hebrews urges believers to run with endurance the race set before them; the explicit need to last through a course closely complements the commentary's horse that preserves running power for the end.

column5: make straight paths for your feet
column6: Hebrews instructs readers to make straight paths for their feet so that the disabled may be healed rather than turned aside, a Christian ethical use of the commentary's smooth, guided gait.
Jesus says that the one who endures to the end will be saved; it gives the commentary's emphasis on what lasts at the end a direct eschatological criterion.
Hebrews says dispossessed believers know they have a better and abiding possession; its paired comparative is exceptionally close to S87:17's “better and more enduring.”
The patriarchs seek a better country, explicitly identified as heavenly; the verse gives the commentary's distant/later destination a pilgrim-country image.

Jesus tells hearers not to work for food that perishes but for food that endures to eternal life, closely matching the commentary's warning against priority for the immediately available and perishable.
Jesus asks what profits someone who gains the whole world but forfeits life; its whole-world versus life calculation is a sharp Gospel counterpart to preference for dunya.

After comparing bodily training with godliness, the verse says godliness promises both the present life and the coming life; it qualifies the commentary's contrast by valuing present life within a future-oriented discipline.
First Peter describes an inheritance as imperishable, undefiled, unfading, and kept in heaven; its safeguarded future good gives a Christian image for S87:17's abiding outcome.

column5: momentary affliction, eternal weight of glory
column6: Paul says momentary, light affliction produces an eternal weight of glory beyond comparison; its time-scale makes the commentary's near/later reversal explicit.

column5: feet like a hind and high places
column6: Habakkuk says the Lord makes his feet like a hind's and lets him tread high places; it is a divine-strength reading of animal footwork, though not a race or file.
The wicked speakers urge one another to enjoy present good things before they pass; their voice gives a specific Jewish portrayal of the immediate-life preference criticized in the commentary.

column5: two spirits in which to walk
column6: The Community Rule says God assigned humanity spirits of truth and perversity in which to walk until visitation; it develops divine ordering, directed walking, and divergent outcomes without the animal imagery.

column5: works prepared beforehand to walk in
column6: Believers are created for good works that God prepared beforehand so they might walk in them; it offers a Christian formulation of a divinely prepared and guided way.
Hebrews rereads Esau's sale of his birthright for one meal as a warning against irreverence, giving the immediate-versus-lasting choice in Gen.25 a Christian moral interpretation.

Jude calls false teachers wandering stars reserved for deepest darkness; as a moral inversion of the commentary's stars moving in ordered courses, it is image-based rather than an astronomical parallel.

column5: two ways of life and death
column6: The Didache's opening formula distinguishes a way of life from a way of death; it is a Christian two-way framework beside S87:3, 8, and 16-17, though it does not share the running-file scene.
